parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The output of a power supply is represented by:

$$V = 9.0 \sin 20t$$

where $V$ is the potential difference in volts and $t$ is the time in seconds.

Determine, for the output of the supply:
hints: Hint 1: Look at the form $V = 9.0 \sin 20t$. The number in front of $\sin$ is the maximum value the voltage ever reaches. Think about whether r.m.s. should be larger or smaller than this peak value because it represents the equivalent heating effect.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Peak Voltage**
For a sinusoidal supply, the equation has the form $$V = V_0 \sin \omega t$$ where $V_0$ is the peak or maximum voltage. Here $V_0 = 9.0\text{ V}$.

Step 2: **Convert Peak to R.M.S.**
For a sine wave only, the r.m.s. value is smaller than the peak by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$: $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ So $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{9.0}{\sqrt{2}} = 6.4\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Compare $V = 9.0 \sin 20t$ with the standard form $V = V_0 \sin \omega t$. Identify what the number 20 represents physically in terms of how fast the cycle repeats.
Hint 2: Recall how angular frequency $\omega$ in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ is linked to period $T$ for one full oscillation. Rearrange that link to find $T$ from $\omega = 20$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify Angular Frequency**
Comparing $$V = 9.0 \sin 20t \text{ with } V = V_0 \sin \omega t$$ gives $$\omega = 20\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ This $\omega$ tells you how many radians of the sine cycle are covered per second.

Step 2: **Use Period Relation**
One full cycle is $2\pi$ radians, so: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ Rearranging before putting numbers in: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{20} = 0.31\text{ s}$$

hints: Hint 1: Power in a resistor depends on the heating effect, which is set by $V_{r.m.s.}$, not just the peak $V_0$. Look at Fig. 9.1 and Fig. 9.2 - even though the peaks look the same height, does the square wave spend more time near the peak than the sine wave?
parts.proper_answer: No. The r.m.s. voltages are different so the powers $P = V_{r.m.s.}^2 / R$ are different.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Power Is Set By R.M.S.**
In a resistor the mean power is $$P = \frac{V_{r.m.s.}^2}{R}$$ So two supplies give the same power only if their $V_{r.m.s.}$ values are the same.

Step 2: **Compare the Waveforms**
Both graphs have the same peak $V_0$, but the square wave in Fig. 9.2 stays at $\pm V_0$ all the time, while the sine wave in Fig. 9.1 is only briefly at the peak. That means the square wave has a larger r.m.s. value, $V_0$, compared to $V_0/\sqrt{2}$ for the sine wave. Different $V_{r.m.s.}$ means different power, so the answer is no.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text:
The power supply in (a) is connected to a transformer. The input power to the transformer is $80\text{W}$.

The secondary coil is connected to a resistor. The r.m.s. voltage across the resistor is $120\text{V}$. The r.m.s. current in the secondary coil is $0.64\text{A}$.

Calculate the efficiency of the transformer.
hints: Hint 1: Efficiency always means useful power out divided by power in. Identify which 80 W is, and which side of the transformer you need to calculate power for.
Hint 2: For the secondary connected to a resistor, the output power can be found from the r.m.s. readings. Think about how $V_{r.m.s.}$ and $I_{r.m.s.}$ combine to give mean power.
Hint 3: Once you have output power in watts, divide by the 80 W input and multiply by 100 to express efficiency as a percentage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Useful Output Power**
For a resistive load, r.m.s. values give the real mean power directly: $$P_{out} = V_{r.m.s.} I_{r.m.s.}$$ So $$P_{out} = 120 \times 0.64 = 76.8\text{ W}$$

Step 2: **Apply Efficiency Definition**
Efficiency compares what you get out to what you put in: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} \times 100\%$$

Step 3: **Calculate the Value**
$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{76.8}{80} \times 100\% = 0.96 = 96\%$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: State **one** reason why the transformer is not 100% efficient.

markscheme_points.text: Any one from: • heat losses due to resistance of windings / coils • heat losses in magnetising and demagnetising • heat losses due to eddy currents in (iron) core • loss of flux linkage

hints: Hint 1: If output power is less than input power, some energy must be going somewhere else. Think about heating in the wires and in the iron core when currents and changing magnetism are present.
parts.proper_answer: Heat loss due to resistance of coils, or eddy currents in core, or hysteresis loss in magnetising core, or flux leakage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where Does Lost Energy Go?**
A real transformer warms up. Any one valid loss mechanism earns credit. For example, the copper windings have resistance so $I^2R$ heating occurs, changing currents induce eddy currents in the iron core causing heating, energy is needed to repeatedly magnetise and demagnetise the core (hysteresis), or not all primary flux links the secondary.
